lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "When you type a URL or an app fetches data, your device first looks up the server's IP address using DNS (like a phonebook). Then it opens a reliable pipe (TCP), locks it with encryption (TLS/HTTPS), and sends a structured text message (an HTTP Request with Method, Path, Headers, and JSON Body). The Go backend reads that message, checks if you are allowed, updates the database, and replies with an HTTP Status Code (like 200 OK or 404 Not Found) and JSON data.", "intermediate": "At the transport and application layers, an HTTPS request requires DNS resolution, a 1-RTT TCP 3-way handshake, and a 1-RTT TLS 1.3 handshake before application bytes flow. In Go's net/http package, http.Server spawns a dedicated goroutine per accepted *net.TCPConn, reusing that goroutine across multiple requests on the same HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connection or spawning per-stream goroutines in HTTP/2. REST API contracts rely on idempotent HTTP methods (GET, PUT, DELETE vs non-idempotent POST) and strict JSON serialization via encoding/json.", "advanced": "Internally, Go's net.Conn.Read calls into internal/poll.FD.Read, which performs a non-blocking read syscall. If the socket buffer is empty (syscall.EAGAIN), the runtime invokes runtime.gopark, registering the file descriptor with epoll_ctl(EPOLL_CTL_ADD/MOD) with edge-triggered EPOLLET events and detaching the Goroutine (G) from its OS Thread (M) so the Processor (P) immediately executes other runnable goroutines. Compared to Java NIO selector threads or Node.js single-threaded libuv callbacks, Go gives you synchronous imperative code with asynchronous non-blocking epoll efficiency."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
[Client / Browser]
   │ 1. DNS Lookup (UDP/53 or DoH) -> Resolves api.example.com to 203.0.113.42
   │ 2. TCP 3-Way Handshake (SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK) [1 RTT]
   │ 3. TLS 1.3 Handshake (ClientHello + KeyShare -> ServerHello + Cert + Finished) [1 RTT]
   ▼
[Reverse Proxy: Caddy / Nginx]  (Terminates TLS, enforces Rate Limit, forwards X-Forwarded-For)
   │ 4. HTTP/1.1 Keep-Alive or HTTP/2 Multiplexed Stream over Local VPC
   ▼
[Go net/http Server]
   ├── Accept Loop (epoll / kqueue network poller wakes Goroutine)
   ├── Middleware Chain (RequestID -> slog Logger -> Panic Recovery -> Auth -> Timeout)
   ├── Handler + DTO Validation (JSON Deserialization & Schema Contract Check)
   └── Connection Pool (database/sql or pgxpool) ──► [PostgreSQL / Redis]
lesson_sections.reasoning: Explicit ReadHeaderTimeout, ReadTimeout, WriteTimeout, and IdleTimeout bound socket lifetime. http.MaxBytesReader aborts reads at the stream level before heap exhaustion, and json.Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields catches client contract drift immediately.
lesson_sections.title: 0.1 Client-Server Architecture, DNS/TCP/TLS & HTTP Request Lifecycle

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "An API Contract is a promise between the backend and frontend: 'If you send me a JSON object with `email` and `amount_cents`, I will return HTTP 201 with an `order_id`.' In Go, struct tags like `` `json:\"amount_cents\"` `` tell Go how to translate between Go structs and JSON text.", "intermediate": "Language Guarantee vs Standard Library Behavior: In Go's `encoding/json`, unexported struct fields (starting with a lowercase letter) are silently ignored during marshaling and unmarshaling! Also, when designing a `PATCH /users/{id}` endpoint for partial updates, use pointer fields (`*string`, `*bool`) in the request DTO so you can check `if req.ReceiveNewsletter != nil` to distinguish 'field was not sent' from 'client explicitly sent `false`'.", "advanced": "Internally, `encoding/json` caches struct encoder functions in a `sync.Map` keyed by `reflect.Type`. However, marshaling via `json.Marshal` allocates a full `[]byte` buffer in memory. For large responses, streaming with `json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v)` writes via an internal pooled buffer, though note that once `w.Write` is called, HTTP status headers can no longer be changed if a marshaling error occurs mid-stream."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
HTTP Method Idempotency & Safety Matrix (RFC 9110):
┌──────────┬─────────┬────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Method   │ Safe?   │ Idempotent?│ Engineering Contract & Retry Behavior                   │
├──────────┼─────────┼────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ GET      │ YES     │ YES        │ Read-only; safe for automatic L7 proxy/client retries   │
│ PUT      │ NO      │ YES        │ Full resource replacement at known URI; safe to retry   │
│ DELETE   │ NO      │ YES        │ Deleting N times leaves resource absent (200/204/404)   │
│ POST     │ NO      │ NO*        │ Creates subordinate resource; requires Idempotency-Key! │
│ PATCH    │ NO      │ NO*        │ Partial modification; idempotent only if setting values │
└──────────┴─────────┴────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
lesson_sections.reasoning: Exported fields (`DisplayName`, `IsActive`) are visible to `encoding/json`, and pointer types (`*string`, `*bool`) remain `nil` when omitted from the JSON payload, preserving existing database values.
lesson_sections.title: 0.3 REST Idempotency, JSON Marshaling Internals & Backward-Compatible API Contracts

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
The Terminal is a text-based way to talk to your computer: `pwd` shows your current folder, `cd` changes folders, and `mkdir` creates a new folder. `git init` starts a time-machine history for your code. `go mod init` creates a `go.mod` ID card for your Go project, and `func main()` inside `package main` is the front door where your program starts running.

[Intermediate Technical]
A Go workspace is anchored by `go.mod`. Executable commands declare `package main` and `func main()`, while reusable libraries declare package names matching their directory names. Separating pure functions from `main()` enables unit testing via `go test`.

[Advanced Internals]
Go compiles directly to native ELF/PE/Mach-O machine code without a virtual machine. `CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -ldflags="-s -w"` produces a statically linked binary that can run inside a 2MB distroless container.

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: The essential developer workflow combining the command-line terminal, Git version control, and the Go toolchain (go mod init, go run, go build, go test).
2. Internal Mechanics: When you run "go run .", the Go toolchain parses go.mod to resolve your module root, compiles all .go files in package main into a temporary native machine-code binary, and executes func main().
3. Why Needed: Backend engineers build, test, and deploy services through the CLI and automated CI pipelines rather than GUI buttons.
4. Why Preferred: Go includes a complete, zero-configuration toolchain (compiler, formatter gofmt, linter go vet, and test runner go test) out of the box.
5. When To Use: At the start of every new Go repository or microservice.
6. When To Avoid: Never write Go code outside a Go module (always initialize go.mod first).
7. Advantages: Fast compilation; reproducible dependency tracking in go.mod/go.sum; safe version history with Git.
8. Disadvantages: Requires familiarity with basic shell commands (cd, ls, mkdir).
9. Alternatives: Makefile or task runners wrapping the underlying go commands.
10. Incorrect Consequences: Using a package name other than "package main" for your entry file causes "go run" to fail because there is no executable entry point.
11. Real-World Usage: Every production Go repository contains a go.mod at its root and entry points under cmd/<service>/main.go.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: Maintainability: Keeping main() thin and moving logic into testable functions lets you verify behavior with go test.
lesson_sections.diagram_text: [Terminal: pwd / cd / mkdir] -> [git init & git commit] -> [go mod init example.com/app] -> [main.go] -> [go run .]
lesson_sections.reasoning: Declaring `package main` provides the executable entry point while `Greeting(name string) string` can be asserted directly in `main_test.go`.
lesson_sections.title: 0.0B Installing Go, Terminal Commands, Git Basics & Your First main.go

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
Think of a restaurant: the dining room menu is the Frontend (what the customer sees), the kitchen is the Backend (where orders are checked and cooked), and the locked vault/pantry is the Database. Customers never walk into the vault—they give their order to the kitchen via a numbered counter window (a Port like 8080).

[Intermediate Technical]
At the OS level, a backend is a long-running user-space process. It reads runtime settings from environment variables via os.Getenv, opens a listening TCP socket on HOST:PORT, and multiplexes incoming client connections across lightweight goroutines.

[Advanced Internals]
Under Linux/Windows, listening on a TCP port allocates a socket file descriptor in the kernel table. Twelve-Factor App architecture mandates strict separation of config from code via environment variables so immutable container images can be promoted from staging to prod.

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: A backend is a program running on a computer (server) that waits for network requests on a specific Port, enforces security and business rules, reads or writes a database, and sends back a structured response.
2. Internal Mechanics: When you start a compiled Go binary, the Operating System creates a Process with a Process ID (PID), virtual memory space, file descriptors, and an environment variable table (os.Getenv). When the process binds to a TCP port (e.g. :8080), the OS kernel routes packets arriving for that port to your process.
3. Why Needed: If a web page or mobile app connected directly to your database, any user could inspect the app, extract the database password, and delete or steal every customer record.
4. Why Preferred: Centralizing rules in a compiled Go server gives you one authoritative boundary for validation, authentication, rate limiting, and database transactions.
5. When To Use: Every web app, mobile app, payment webhook, or multi-user system where data must be shared, validated, and protected.
6. When To Avoid: Purely offline client-side calculators or static brochure pages with no shared state or secrets.
7. Advantages: Protects database credentials; enforces business invariants; compiles to a single fast native binary in Go.
8. Disadvantages: Requires running and monitoring a server process and managing network/database configuration.
9. Alternatives: Static files on a CDN (no dynamic state) or Serverless functions (FaaS, higher cold-start latency).
10. Incorrect Consequences: Hardcoding ports or database passwords inside source code makes the binary impossible to reconfigure across environments and leaks secrets into Git.
11. Real-World Usage: Go Backend Academy itself reads PORT, DB_DRIVER, POSTGRES_PORT, and SQLITE_PATH from .env / environment variables at startup.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: Security: Secrets stay in environment variables, never in Git. Maintainability: One binary runs anywhere by changing .env.
