package main

// BUG: Changing port requires recompiling; password is leaked in Git!
const ServerPort = "8080"
const DatabasePassword = "prod-secret-password"
lesson_sections.diagram_text: [Browser / Mobile App] ---> (IP Address + Port :8080) ---> [Go Server Process (PID)] ---> [Database File / PostgreSQL]
lesson_sections.reasoning: os.Getenv("PORT") allows .env, systemd, Docker, or Kubernetes to inject any port at runtime while falling back to defaultPort in local dev.
lesson_sections.title: 0.0A What is a Backend? Servers, Terminal, Files, Processes & Ports

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "Authentication (AuthN) answers 'Who are you?' (logging in with password or OAuth). Authorization (AuthZ) answers 'What are you allowed to do?' (can User A delete User B's invoice?). A stateless backend doesn't rely on one specific server remembering you in its RAM\u2014any server in the cluster can handle your request.", "intermediate": "When scaling horizontally behind an L7 load balancer, storing session state in a process-local Go map breaks as soon as multiple instances run. Externalizing session state to Redis or verifying cryptographic tokens makes compute nodes cattle, not pets. Similarly, a Modular Monolith enforces strict Go package boundaries (using internal/ packages) inside one binary, avoiding RPC serialization taxes until independent scaling is proven necessary.", "advanced": "Distributed microservices trade in-process function calls (~2ns) and local ACID transactions for gRPC/HTTP calls (~1\u20135ms), partial failures, clock skew, and Saga/Outbox coordination. Start with a Modular Monolith where domain modules communicate via narrow Go interfaces; if one domain later requires 10x CPU scaling, swap the interface implementation from an in-process call to a gRPC client without rewriting domain logic."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
[Load Balancer (Round-Robin / Least-Conn)]
       ├──► [Go API Replica 1 (Stateless)] ──┐
       ├──► [Go API Replica 2 (Stateless)] ──┼──► [Shared State Layer: PostgreSQL + Redis]
       └──► [Go API Replica 3 (Stateless)] ──┘
(Any replica can serve any request without sticky sessions)
lesson_sections.reasoning: Injecting SessionStore decouples compute nodes from local RAM state, and scoping repository queries by both (invoiceID, ownerUserID) makes Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA) impossible by design.
lesson_sections.title: 0.2 Stateless vs Stateful Systems, AuthN vs AuthZ & Monolith vs Microservices

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "In Go, a struct doesn't need to say `implements Reader`. If it has a `Read([]byte) (int, error)` method, it automatically satisfies `io.Reader`! Also, Go doesn't throw exceptions for normal errors\u2014functions return an `error` value as their last result so you handle problems right where they happen.", "intermediate": "Define interfaces on the consumer side ('Accept interfaces, return concrete structs'). When propagating errors up the call stack, wrap them using `fmt.Errorf(\"context: %w\", err)` so callers can still inspect sentinel errors via `errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)` or extract structured error types via `errors.As(err, &validationErr)`.", "advanced": "Understand the `runtime.iface` memory layout: an interface holds `(type, value)`. If a function declares `var err *MyCustomError = nil` and returns `err` as an `error` interface, the returned `iface` has `type = *MyCustomError` and `value = nil`, which evaluates `err != nil` as `true`. Always declare error variables as `var err error` or return explicit `nil`."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
Interface Value (iface = 16 bytes on 64-bit):
┌──────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────┐
│ tab (*itab: concrete type    │ data (unsafe.Pointer to      │
│      + method table)         │       concrete value)        │
└──────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────┘
CRITICAL TRAP: An interface is ONLY nil when BOTH tab == nil AND data == nil!
Assigning (*MyError)(nil) sets tab = *itab(MyError), data = 0x0  ==>  err != nil is TRUE!
lesson_sections.reasoning: Returning `error` directly from `validate` (or checking `if err != nil` before returning) guarantees a true nil interface `(nil, nil)`. Using `errors.Is` walks the entire `Unwrap()` chain safely.
lesson_sections.title: 1.2 Implicit Interfaces, Composition, Errors as Values & Generics

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "In Go, a Slice is like a window looking at an underlying row of boxes (an Array). If two slices look at the same array, changing an item in one window is visible in the other\u2014unless one window grows too big (via append) and moves to a brand-new row of boxes. Also, Go automatically decides whether to put variables on the fast scratchpad (Stack) or the shared warehouse (Heap).", "intermediate": "A slice header is 24 bytes: pointer, length, capacity. When you pass a slice to a function, the header is copied by value, meaning mutations to s[i] mutate the caller's backing array, whereas append(s, x) returns an updated header that must be reassigned. Escape analysis (`go build -gcflags='-m'`) determines at compile time whether a pointer outlives its function or is stored in an interface, promoting it to the heap.", "advanced": "Two classic production memory leaks in Go involve slices and maps: (1) Slicing `header := fullPacket[:20]` retains a pointer into `fullPacket`'s backing array, preventing the tri-color GC from freeing the rest of the multi-megabyte buffer; use `bytes.Clone(fullPacket[:20])` or `copy()` to detach. (2) Go's `runtime.hmap` never releases allocated bucket arrays when keys are deleted via `delete(m, k)`\u2014long-lived caches that spike to 10M keys and delete them all still retain the bucket memory until the map itself is recreated."}
lesson_sections.reasoning: bytes.Clone allocates an exact-sized 16-byte backing array and copies the bytes, allowing the multi-megabyte buffer to be reclaimed on the next GC cycle. make([]string, 0, len(inputs)) eliminates O(log N) array growth copies.
lesson_sections.title: 1.1 Slices, Maps, Pointers, Stack vs Heap & Escape Analysis

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
In Go, `if` makes decisions, `switch` picks between multiple options (and stops automatically without needing `break`), and `for` is the only loop word you ever need. Best of all, a Go function can return two things at once: the answer AND an `error` (which is `nil` when everything succeeded).

[Intermediate Technical]
Go `if` statements support a scoped initialization statement (`if v, err := parse(x); err != nil { return err }`) so temporary variables do not leak into the rest of the function body. Guard clauses validate preconditions first, leaving the main business logic unindented.

[Advanced Internals]
Under Go register-based calling convention (Go 1.17+), multiple return values `(bool, error)` are passed back in CPU registers rather than spilling to the stack, making explicit error returns zero-allocation and faster than stack-unwinding exceptions.

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: Go control structures (`if`, `switch`, `for`) and multi-value function signatures (`(T, error)`).
2. Internal Mechanics: Go has no `while` or `do-while` keywords—`for` handles counter loops (`for i := 0; i < n; i++`), condition loops (`for cond`), and infinite loops (`for {}`). Functions return multiple values directly on the call stack or CPU registers.
3. Why Needed: Every backend handler must validate inputs, branch on business rules, loop over records, and report errors clearly to its caller.
4. Why Preferred: Returning `(result, error)` forces callers to acknowledge failure paths at the call site instead of letting hidden exceptions crash the process.
5. When To Use: Use early-return guard clauses at the top of functions and `(T, error)` for any operation that can fail.
6. When To Avoid: Avoid deeply nested `if/else` pyramids; return early on invalid conditions.
7. Advantages: No accidental switch fallthrough; no hidden control-flow jumps from exceptions; crystal-clear error paths.
8. Disadvantages: Requires explicit `if err != nil` checks.
9. Alternatives: Table-driven lookup maps when branching across dozens of static keys.
10. Incorrect Consequences: Ignoring a returned error or conflating invalid input with a normal `false` result hides bugs.
11. Real-World Usage: Every repository and validator function in Go Backend Academy returns `(T, error)` and uses guard clauses.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: Maintainability: Guard clauses keep cyclomatic complexity low and make security checks obvious during code review.
lesson_sections.diagram_text: func ValidateAccountAge(age int) (bool, error) -> [Guard: age < 0 || age > 130] -> [Check: age < 18] -> return true, nil
lesson_sections.reasoning: The first guard clause rejects impossible inputs with an explicit error; the second handles valid under-18 users; the final line returns adult approval.
lesson_sections.title: 1.0B Conditionals (if/switch), For Loops, Functions & Multiple Return Values

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
An **Interface** is a job description: "anything with a `Read(p []byte) (int, error)` method is an `io.Reader`." You do not have to write `implements`—if your struct has the method, it gets the job! The most famous interface in Go is `error`. When an error happens, wrap it with `fmt.Errorf("context: %w", err)` so callers can still check the original cause with `errors.Is`.

[Intermediate Technical]
Sentinel errors (`var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")`) represent expected domain conditions. Wrapping them with `%w` constructs an error chain that `errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound)` traverses automatically. Use `defer f.Close()` right after checking `f, err := os.Open(...)` so the file descriptor never leaks.

[Advanced Internals]
In Go 1.20+, `errors.Join(errs...)` combines multiple validation errors into a single error whose `Unwrap() []error` method works seamlessly with `errors.Is` and `errors.As` (used in `config.Load()`).

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: Implicit behavioral contracts (`interface`), structured error chains (`error`, `%w`, `errors.Is`), and scoped resource cleanup (`defer`).
2. Internal Mechanics: Any type that defines the methods listed in an interface satisfies it automatically at compile time. `error` is a built-in interface with one method: `Error() string`. `defer` pushes a cleanup call onto the current goroutine frame so it runs even if the function returns early.
3. Why Needed: Interfaces let your HTTP handlers and services depend on small contracts (like `curriculum.Repository`) instead of hard-wiring a concrete database driver, and `%w` error wrapping preserves root causes across layers.
4. Why Preferred: Consumer-defined interfaces keep packages decoupled without heavyweight Java/C# inheritance hierarchies.
5. When To Use: Define small 1-to-4 method interfaces in the consumer package, wrap lower-level errors with `fmt.Errorf("doing X: %w", err)`, and `defer rows.Close()` immediately after opening a resource.
6. When To Avoid: Do not create huge 20-method interfaces before you have a real consumer or test fake.
7. Advantages: Effortless unit testing with in-memory fakes; preserved error chains; leak-free resource cleanup with `defer`.
8. Disadvantages: Returning a typed `nil` pointer as an `error` interface creates a non-nil interface value (covered in depth in Lesson 1.2).
9. Alternatives: Concrete struct dependencies for purely internal helper utilities.
10. Incorrect Consequences: Formatting errors with `%v` or `%s` instead of `%w` breaks `errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows)`, turning 404 Not Found responses into 500 Internal Server Errors.
11. Real-World Usage: `internal/modules/curriculum/service.go`, `lessons/service.go`, and `assessments/service.go` all define small consumer `Repository` interfaces satisfied by `*database.Store`.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: Maintainability: Adding context at each boundary (`"querying user %s: %w"`) produces self-explanatory logs without noisy stack traces.
lesson_sections.diagram_text: Repository Interface <-- (satisfied implicitly by *database.Store & * FakeRepo) | fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err) -> errors.Is
lesson_sections.reasoning: Returning `ErrEmptyOrderID` for missing IDs and wrapping `cause` with `%w` preserves full `errors.Is` inspectability.
lesson_sections.title: 1.0E Interfaces, Explicit Error Handling, Custom Errors & Defer

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
When a browser sends JSON like `{"title":"Learn Go","done":false}`, Go uses `json.Unmarshal` to fill a struct. Two golden rules: (1) Field names inside the struct MUST start with a Capital letter (`Title`, `Done`) so `encoding/json` is allowed to see them, and (2) always pass a pointer (`&in`) to `json.Unmarshal` so it can fill your struct!

[Intermediate Technical]
Struct tags like `` `json:"title"` `` map snake_case or lowercase JSON keys to PascalCase Go fields, and `` `json:"missing,omitempty"` `` omits empty fields from responses. Unit tests live alongside code in `*_test.go` and fail via `t.Errorf` or `t.Fatalf`.

[Advanced Internals]
To prevent silent contract drift on incoming HTTP requests, wrap the stream in `http.MaxBytesReader` and use `dec := json.NewDecoder(r.Body); dec.DisallowUnknownFields()` followed by a second EOF check (`internal/platform/http/router.go:decodeJSON`).

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: Translating between JSON payloads and Go structs using `encoding/json`, reading configuration/files via `os`, and verifying code with `testing.T`.
2. Internal Mechanics: `encoding/json` uses reflection to map JSON object keys to exported (Capitalized) struct fields decorated with `` `json:"field_name"` `` tags. `go test` compiles files ending in `_test.go` and runs every `func TestXxx(t *testing.T)`.
3. Why Needed: REST APIs communicate in JSON, and no backend function is trustworthy until an automated unit test proves both its happy path and error cases.
4. Why Preferred: Go standard `encoding/json` and `testing` packages require zero third-party assertion or serialization dependencies.
5. When To Use: On every API request/response DTO and every package in your repository.
6. When To Avoid: Never use lowercase (unexported) struct fields on JSON DTOs—`encoding/json` will silently ignore them.
7. Advantages: Zero external dependencies; built-in `go test -v -race` execution; clear struct tag mapping.
8. Disadvantages: Reflection-based JSON decoding is slower than streaming decoders if huge payloads are not bounded.
9. Alternatives: Streaming `json.NewDecoder(r.Body)` with `DisallowUnknownFields()` for HTTP request bodies.
10. Incorrect Consequences: Lowercase struct fields result in empty/zero values after `json.Unmarshal` with no error returned, causing silent data loss.
11. Real-World Usage: Used in `tests/server_integration_test.go` and all DTOs in `internal/shared/`.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: Quality: Running `go test -v ./...` catches regressions in sub-second time.
lesson_sections.diagram_text: JSON Bytes ---> json.Unmarshal(raw, &dto) ---> Exported Fields (`json:"title"`) ---> Validated Domain Struct ---> *_test.go
lesson_sections.reasoning: Exported `Title` and `Done` fields are populated by `json.Unmarshal(raw, &in)`, and `in.Title == ""` rejects blank titles immediately.
lesson_sections.title: 1.0F JSON Struct Tags, File I/O, Environment Variables & Your First Go Test

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
A **Slice** (`[]string{"paid", "pending"}`) is a numbered list that can grow with `append()`. A **Map** (`map[string]int`) is a dictionary that connects a Key (like `"paid"`) to a Value (like `3`). Important rule: before putting items into a map, you must create it with `make(map[string]int)` or `map[string]int{}`!

[Intermediate Technical]
When iterating a slice or map with `for k, v := range col`, `v` is a copy of the element. For maps, reading a missing key returns the value type zero value without panicking; use `v, ok := m[k]` when you need to know whether the key was actually present.

[Advanced Internals]
Pre-allocating `make(map[string]int, hint)` computes the required bucket logarithm `B` up front in `runtime.makemap`, eliminating incremental evacuation pauses during bulk inserts.

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: Go two primary collection types: Slices (`[]T`) for ordered sequences and Maps (`map[K]V`) for key-value lookups.
2. Internal Mechanics: A slice is a 24-byte header (`ptr`, `len`, `cap`) pointing to a contiguous backing array. A map is a pointer to a runtime hash table (`runtime.hmap`) organized into buckets of 8 key/value slots.
3. Why Needed: Almost every API endpoint returns a list of items (a slice) or aggregates/looks up records by ID or status (a map).
4. Why Preferred: Slices offer cache-friendly contiguous memory, while built-in maps provide O(1) average lookup with randomized hash seeds to prevent hash-flooding DoS.
5. When To Use: Use `[]T` for ordered collections and JSON arrays; use `map[K]V` for deduplication, frequency counting, and O(1) key lookups.
6. When To Avoid: Never write to an uninitialized (`nil`) map, and never share a map across concurrent goroutines without a `sync.RWMutex`.
7. Advantages: Ergonomic `append()`, `len()`, `for i, v := range`, and `val, ok := m[key]` syntax.
8. Disadvantages: Map iteration order is intentionally randomized by the Go runtime.
9. Alternatives: Sorted slices with `slices.BinarySearch` for small read-heavy lookup tables.
10. Incorrect Consequences: Declaring `var m map[string]int` and writing `m["k"] = 1` crashes the goroutine with `panic: assignment to entry in nil map`.
11. Real-World Usage: Used in `config.Load()` for `CORSAllowedOrigins map[string]bool` and in `Store.GetUserProgress` for lesson status maps.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: Performance: Pre-sizing with `make([]T, 0, n)` or `make(map[K]V, n)` avoids repeated reallocations.
lesson_sections.diagram_text: Slice ([]string) -> ordered list | Map (make(map[string]int)) -> key/value lookup with v, ok := m[k]
lesson_sections.reasoning: `make(map[string]int, len(items))` initializes the hash table so `counts[s]++` safely reads the zero value (0) and stores 1.
lesson_sections.title: 1.0C Working with Collections: Arrays, Slices, Maps & Range Loops

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
A **Struct** is a custom blueprint that groups fields together (like a `Wallet` having a `BalanceCents` field). By default, Go hands functions a *photocopy* of a struct. If you want a method to update the *original* `Wallet` instead of a photocopy, you use a **Pointer** (`*Wallet`), which points to the original box in memory.

[Intermediate Technical]
The `&` operator takes the address of a variable (`w := &Wallet{}`), producing a `*Wallet` pointer. For struct pointers, Go automatically dereferences field access (`w.BalanceCents` is shorthand for `(*w).BalanceCents`). Keep receiver types consistent across all methods of a type.

[Advanced Internals]
Calling a method on a `nil` struct pointer does not panic at the call site—it enters the method with receiver `w == nil`, allowing the method itself to check `if w == nil` and return a graceful error (exactly how `(*Store).Ping` works).

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: Composite data modeling with `struct` types, methods, and explicit memory pointers (`*T` and `&x`).
2. Internal Mechanics: Go passes every function argument and method receiver by value (copying it). When a method declares a pointer receiver `(w *Wallet)`, Go copies the 8-byte memory address so `w.BalanceCents += amt` updates the original struct in place.
3. Why Needed: Backend services model domain entities (`Server`, `Store`, `Order`, `Config`) as structs with methods that encapsulate state transitions.
4. Why Preferred: Explicit pointers (`*T`) vs values (`T`) let you see at the type signature whether a function can mutate your struct or be `nil`.
5. When To Use: Use pointer receivers (`*T`) when a method mutates the receiver or when the struct is large or contains a `sync.Mutex`.
6. When To Avoid: Do not use pointers for small immutable value types like `time.Time` or 2-field coordinate structs.
7. Advantages: Zero hidden boxing; contiguous struct field memory layout; explicit mutability.
8. Disadvantages: Dereferencing a `nil` pointer causes a runtime panic if not guarded.
9. Alternatives: Returning a new updated struct value `(Wallet, error)` in purely functional domain models.
10. Incorrect Consequences: Using a value receiver `(w Wallet)` on a mutating method modifies a temporary copy that is immediately discarded when the method returns.
11. Real-World Usage: `*database.Store` and `*httpplatform.Server` use pointer receivers across all methods.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: Reliability: Guarding `if w == nil` at API boundaries prevents nil-dereference crashes.
lesson_sections.diagram_text: type Wallet struct { BalanceCents int64 } ---> func (w *Wallet) Deposit(amt int64) error (mutates original via pointer)
lesson_sections.reasoning: The pointer receiver `*Wallet` updates the caller struct in place, while `w == nil` and `amountCents <= 0` enforce domain invariants.
lesson_sections.title: 1.0D Structs, Methods, Value vs Pointer Receivers & Safe Nil Checks

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
A variable is a labeled box in memory that holds a specific kind of data (its Type): whole numbers (`int`, `int64`), decimals (`float64`), true/false (`bool`), or text (`string`). Inside a function, `count := 10` creates and fills the box in one step. If you create an empty box with `var count int`, Go automatically puts `0` inside—never random garbage.

[Intermediate Technical]
Go enforces strict nominal and structural typing with zero implicit numeric coercion: adding an `int` and an `int64` is a compile error unless converted (`int64(a) + b`). Strings are immutable UTF-8 byte views; indexing `s[i]` yields a `byte` (`uint8`), while iterating with `range` decodes `rune` (`int32`) Unicode code points.

[Advanced Internals]
The Go Language Specification ("The zero value") guarantees zero-initialization for all allocated storage. The compiler optimizes stack allocations using CPU register assignments (SSA form) and zeroes heap blocks in bulk via `runtime.mallocgc`.

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: Go static type system and variable initialization rules that guarantee every variable in memory starts with a known, deterministic value.
2. Internal Mechanics: When memory is allocated on the stack or heap in Go, it is zeroed before your code sees it: numeric types are 0, booleans are false, strings are "" (len 0), and pointers/slices/maps/interfaces are nil.
3. Why Needed: Uninitialized variables in C/C++ contain random leftover bytes that cause unpredictable bugs and security leaks. Go eliminates uninitialized memory by language specification.
4. Why Preferred: Explicit integer widths (`int64`, `uint32`) and zero-value guarantees make financial, network protocol, and database code predictable.
5. When To Use: Use `var x T` when starting from the zero value, and `x := expr` when initializing from an expression inside a function.
6. When To Avoid: Never use `float64` to store or calculate currency/money—use `int64` minor units (cents/rupiah) to prevent binary rounding errors.
7. Advantages: Compile-time type safety; zero uninitialized memory bugs; clear distinction between `byte` (uint8) and `rune` (int32 Unicode code point).
8. Disadvantages: Go forbids implicit numeric conversions (you must write `int64(x)` explicitly).
9. Alternatives: Arbitrary-precision decimal libraries (`shopspring/decimal`) for multi-currency FX rates.
10. Incorrect Consequences: Using `float64` for money causes `0.1 + 0.2` to equal `0.30000000000000004`, breaking ledger reconciliation.
11. Real-World Usage: All order totals in Go Backend Academy (`orders.total_cents`) use `int64` cents.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: Performance: `int64` arithmetic executes in a single CPU clock cycle with zero heap allocation.
lesson_sections.diagram_text: var n int -> 0 | var ok bool -> false | var s string -> "" | Short init: total := priceCents * qty
lesson_sections.reasoning: Storing and multiplying integer cents in `int64` is exact up to 92 quadrillion dollars and prevents negative totals via explicit guards.
lesson_sections.title: 1.0A Go Variables, Primitive Types, Zero Values & Formatting (fmt)

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "In Go, any function, struct, or variable starting with a **Capital Letter** (`User`, `GetByID`) is public (exported) to other packages, while **lowercase** (`parseToken`) is private to its package. Furthermore, any code placed inside an `internal/` folder cannot be imported by outside projects!", "intermediate": "Go Modules (`go.mod` + `go.sum`) use Minimal Version Selection (MVS): if Module A requires `lib v1.2.0` and Module B requires `lib v1.4.0`, Go always picks `v1.4.0`\u2014the oldest version that satisfies all requirements\u2014without guessing or auto-upgrading to `v1.9.0` behind your back.", "advanced": "Runtime Memory Detail: On 64-bit architectures, an `int64` or pointer (`*T`) must be aligned on an 8-byte boundary. Placing `bool` (1 byte) before `int64` (8 bytes) and another `bool` (1 byte) forces the compiler to insert 14 bytes of invisible padding, turning a 10-byte payload into a 24-byte struct. Sorting fields from 8-byte down to 1-byte types packs the struct into 16 bytes."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
64-Bit Struct Field Padding & Alignment (8-byte word boundaries):
❌ Poor Field Order (24 bytes per struct):       ✅ Optimal Field Order (16 bytes per struct - 33% smaller!):
┌──────┬───────────────────────┐                 ┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ bool │ 7 bytes wasted pad    │ (Word 1: 8B)    │ int64 (8 bytes)              │ (Word 1: 8B)
├──────┴───────────────────────┤                 ├──────┬──────┬────────────────┤
│ int64 (8 bytes)              │ (Word 2: 8B)    │ int32│ bool │ bool │ 2B pad  │ (Word 2: 8B)
├──────┬───────────────────────┤                 └──────┴──────┴────────────────┘
│ bool │ 7 bytes wasted pad    │ (Word 3: 8B)
└──────┴───────────────────────┘
lesson_sections.reasoning: Using `const DefaultTimeout = 30 * time.Second` provides compile-time immutability and unit safety (`time.Duration`), while ordering `int64` before `bool` saves 8 bytes per struct instance.
lesson_sections.title: 1.0 Go Toolchain, Module Minimal Version Selection (MVS), internal/ Packages & Struct Layout

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "When deploying a Go app with Docker, don't ship the giant 800MB Go compiler image to your production server! Use a **Multi-Stage Dockerfile**: Stage 1 compiles your Go code into a single binary file, and Stage 2 copies *only* that binary into a tiny, locked-down image (`distroless`) that runs as a non-root user.", "intermediate": "Understand the difference between Kubernetes **Liveness** (`/healthz`) and **Readiness** (`/readyz`) probes: Liveness asks 'Is this process deadlocked and needing a reboot?' while Readiness asks 'Should the load balancer send user traffic to this pod right now?'. If your database briefly slows down and `/healthz` checks the database, Kubernetes will kill and restart all your pods at once!", "advanced": "Tune the Go runtime for Linux cgroups: 1) Set `GOMEMLIMIT` to 85\u201390% of the container's memory limit (e.g., `450MiB` for a `512MiB` pod) so the GC paces mark cycles before the Linux OOM killer strikes (see the official Go GC Guide). 2) For CPU-throttled containers (`resources.limits.cpu`), ensure `GOMAXPROCS` matches the container's integer CPU quota rather than the host node's 64 cores to avoid excessive OS thread context switching."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
Kubernetes Liveness vs Readiness Probe Separation (CRITICAL!):
┌──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Probe Endpoint       │ What It Must Check        │ Kubernetes Action on Failure                 │
├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ GET /healthz         │ Local process alive only  │ Restarts Container (kills pod!)              │
│ (Liveness Probe)     │ (NEVER check DB/Redis!)   │                                              │
├──────────────────────┼───────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ GET /readyz          │ DB Ping + Shutdown Flag   │ Removes Pod IP from Service Load Balancer    │
│ (Readiness Probe)    │ (Checks dependencies)     │ (Does NOT restart pod; prevents cascade!)    │
└──────────────────────┴───────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
lesson_sections.reasoning: When `shuttingDown` flips to `true` on `SIGTERM` or PostgreSQL briefly blips, `/readyz` returns 503 so Kubernetes stops routing traffic to the pod while `/healthz` remains 200 OK, keeping the process alive to finish draining work and reconnect automatically.
lesson_sections.title: 10.1 Multi-Stage Distroless Docker Builds, Kubernetes Probes, Caddy/Nginx & Disaster Recovery

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "In production, you usually put a **Reverse Proxy** like **Caddy** or **Nginx** in front of your Go server to handle HTTPS certificates automatically and forward traffic to `localhost:8080`. Because the Go server sees the connection coming from the proxy (`127.0.0.1`), the proxy passes the user's real IP in a header\u2014but your Go code must verify the request actually came from your proxy before trusting that header!", "intermediate": "How does an attacker spoof `X-Forwarded-For`? If an attacker sends `X-Forwarded-For: 8.8.8.8`, a standard proxy appends the attacker's real IP to the end: `X-Forwarded-For: 8.8.8.8, 203.0.113.99`. If your Go code naively grabs the *first* IP (`8.8.8.8`), the attacker can pretend to be any IP address! Instead, only trust `X-Forwarded-For` when `r.RemoteAddr` is a trusted proxy, and read from the **rightmost** entry.", "advanced": "Disaster Recovery is defined by two concrete metrics: **RPO (Recovery Point Objective)**\u2014how many seconds/minutes of data loss can the business tolerate (e.g., RPO=0 with synchronous WAL standby, or RPO<60s with continuous WAL archiving)\u2014and **RTO (Recovery Time Objective)**\u2014how many minutes until service is restored after a full region/host loss. Document and rehearse your exact runbook (`pgBackRest` restore + DNS cutover) so RTO is measured, not guessed."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
Reverse Proxy X-Forwarded-For Spoofing Defense:
[Attacker] ── Sends fake header: "X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4" ──► [Caddy / Nginx Edge Proxy]
                                                                     │ Appends true socket IP: "1.2.3.4, 203.0.113.88"
                                                                     ▼
[Go Backend] (ONLY trusts X-Forwarded-For if RemoteAddr is in TrustedProxyCIDRs, and reads RIGHTMOST untrusted IP!)
lesson_sections.reasoning: Walking right-to-left across `X-Forwarded-For` after verifying that the TCP peer (`remoteIP`) is a trusted reverse proxy extracts the true IP appended by your edge proxy, ignoring any fake values prepended by the client.
lesson_sections.title: 10.2 Caddy & Nginx Reverse Proxies, Trusted X-Forwarded-For, Canary Rollbacks & Disaster Recovery

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
Here is how everything you have learned fits together into **8 Progressive Capstone Milestones**:
1. **Stage B Capstone**: CLI Task Tracker with JSON File Persistence & Unit Tests
2. **Stage D Capstone**: Hardened `net/http` REST API with Timeouts & Strict JSON Validation
3. **Stage E Capstone**: SQLite/PostgreSQL Repository with Versioned Up/Down Migrations
4. **Stage G Capstone**: Argon2id Authentication, Session/JWT Middleware & BOLA Ownership Guards
5. **Stage F Capstone**: Bounded Worker Pool & Token-Bucket Rate Limiter with Context Cancellation
6. **Stage H Capstone**: Redis Cache-Aside + Singleflight Stampede Protection
7. **Stage H Capstone**: Double-Entry Ledger & Transactional Outbox Relay
8. **Stage I Capstone**: Distroless Docker + `/healthz` vs `/readyz` + Graceful Shutdown

[Intermediate Technical]
At each capstone milestone, verify three things: (1) Happy-path contract tests, (2) Negative/invalid payload rejection (`400`/`401`/`404`/`413`), and (3) Infrastructure failure behavior (DB down -> `/readyz` returns `503`; process restart -> data persists in SQLite/PostgreSQL).

[Advanced Internals]
During a rolling deployment, Kubernetes sends `SIGTERM` to the old pod while simultaneously polling `/readyz`. Marking `ShuttingDown = true` immediately causes `/readyz` to return `503`, removing the pod from `EndpointSlice` before `httpServer.Shutdown(ctx)` finishes draining active requests.

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: The 8-milestone Capstone Synthesis program that guides you from a simple command-line tool to a production-hardened Go backend service.
2. Internal Mechanics: Each milestone layers one new architectural boundary onto the previous one: CLI -> HTTP -> SQL Persistence & Migrations -> Security -> Concurrency -> Caching -> Distributed Reliability -> Container & Kubernetes Readiness.
3. Why Needed: Reading lessons in isolation is not enough; engineers build confidence by assembling complete services and verifying how they behave under failure.
4. Why Preferred: Incremental milestones prevent overwhelm while ensuring every layer (config, DB, HTTP, auth, observability) is genuinely wired and tested.
5. When To Use: As your portfolio capstone progression after completing each curriculum stage.
6. When To Avoid: Do not jump to Milestone 7 (Outbox/Saga) before completing Milestones 1–3 (CLI, HTTP CRUD, SQL Migrations).
7. Advantages: Clear, verifiable deliverables; aligns directly with the 14 production Case Studies in this platform.
8. Disadvantages: Requires writing real tests (`go test -v -race ./...`) at every milestone.
9. Alternatives: Building a single throwaway toy CRUD app with no migrations, timeouts, or readiness checks.
10. Incorrect Consequences: Reporting `200 OK` on `/readyz` when the database is unreachable or migrations have not run causes load balancers to route live traffic into a broken instance.
11. Real-World Usage: Go Backend Academy itself implements Milestone 8: `.env`-driven config, fail-fast DB startup, embedded versioned migrations, strict JSON decoding, and real `/readyz` pings.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: Production Readiness: Fail fast on startup misconfiguration; drain in-flight requests on `SIGTERM` before closing the DB pool.
lesson_sections.diagram_text: [M1: CLI Tool] -> [M2: HTTP CRUD] -> [M3: SQL + Migrations] -> [M4: AuthN/RBAC] -> [M5: Worker Pool] -> [M6: Redis Singleflight] -> [M7: Outbox/Saga] -> [M8: K8s Production]
lesson_sections.reasoning: Returning `503` whenever `ShuttingDown`, `!DBConnected`, or `!MigrationsUp` ensures only healthy, migrated instances receive traffic.
lesson_sections.title: 10.3 Progressive Capstone Roadmap: From CLI & CRUD API to Production Distributed Service

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "A Goroutine (`go fn()`) is an ultra-lightweight background worker managed by Go\u2014you can run 50,000 of them on a laptop. Channels (`chan T`) are typed pipes that let goroutines hand data to each other safely, while `context.Context` is a cancel button that tells all child workers to stop immediately if the user disconnects or times out.", "intermediate": "An unbuffered channel (`make(chan T)`) requires sender and receiver to rendezvous simultaneously; a buffered channel (`make(chan T, N)`) only blocks the sender when the buffer is full. Always use a `select` statement checking `case <-ctx.Done():` alongside channel sends/receives so goroutines exit cleanly when a request is canceled.", "advanced": "Channel operations acquire an internal `hchan.lock` mutex and copy values (unless passing pointers). For simple state protection (like a local cache or counter), `sync.Mutex`, `sync.RWMutex`, or `atomic.Int64` avoids `hchan` scheduling overhead. Furthermore, whenever spawning a child goroutine that writes a single result back to a parent waiting on a `select` with `<-ctx.Done()`, always allocate a buffered channel of size 1 (`make(chan result, 1)`) so the child can deposit its result and exit even if the parent already timed out."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
Go Runtime GMP Work-Stealing Scheduler:
  [P0 (Logical Processor, GOMAXPROCS)]           [P1 (Logical Processor)]
      │ Local Run Queue: [G2, G3, G4]                │ Local Run Queue: [] (Empty -> Steals half from P0!)
      ▼                                              ▼
  [M0 (OS Kernel Thread)]                        [M1 (OS Kernel Thread)]
      │ Executing G1                                 │ Executing Stolen G4
      └──► If G1 blocks on Network/Channel, G1 parks & M0 immediately runs G2!
lesson_sections.reasoning: Sizing the single-producer channel to `make(chan string, 1)` decouples the child goroutine's exit from the parent's `select` branch. Once the child writes to the 1-slot buffer and exits, the channel and buffer become unreachable and are cleanly garbage collected.
lesson_sections.title: 2.1 GMP Scheduler, Channels, Select, Mutexes, Context & Bounded Worker Pools

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "Before trying to make code 'faster', measure it! Go includes a built-in profiler called `pprof` that shows you a map (Flamegraph) of which functions use the most CPU or create the most memory garbage.", "intermediate": "Understand the two Heap Profile modes in `pprof`: 1) `--inuse_space` shows memory that is still alive right now (use this to find memory leaks); 2) `--alloc_space` shows total memory allocated over time even if already freed by the GC (use this to find functions causing high Garbage Collector CPU usage).", "advanced": "When pooling buffers with `sync.Pool`: 1) Always `Reset()` the buffer before `Put`ting it back (or immediately after `Get`), or User B may read User A's leftover bytes! 2) Guard against pooling abnormally huge buffers (e.g., if `buf.Cap() > 64<<10`, drop it instead of returning it to `sync.Pool`) so a single 20MB spike doesn't pin 20MB buffers across all `P` caches."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
Go Profiling & Diagnostics Spectrum:
┌──────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Profile Type         │ What Question Does It Answer?                                  │
├──────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ CPU Profile          │ Where is the program spending active CPU cycles (on-CPU)?      │
│ Heap (inuse_space)   │ What live objects are currently retained in RAM (memory leaks)?│
│ Heap (alloc_space)   │ What functions allocate the most temporary garbage (GC churn)? │
│ Goroutine Profile    │ Are 50,000 goroutines parked waiting on a leaked channel/lock? │
│ Mutex / Block Profile│ Which sync.Mutex or channel is serializing concurrent workers? │
└──────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
lesson_sections.reasoning: Hoisting `regexp.MustCompile` to package initialization reduces allocations per call to zero, and binding `pprof` to an explicit `127.0.0.1` admin `ServeMux` prevents accidental public exposure.
lesson_sections.title: 2.2 CPU & Heap Profiling (pprof), sync.Pool, Contention Profiling & Execution Tracer

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
Imagine cooking breakfast: doing it **sequentially** means toasting bread (2 mins), waiting until it finishes, and only then boiling water (3 mins) = 5 mins total. **Concurrency** means starting the toaster (`go toastBread()`), immediately starting the kettle (`go boilWater()`), and waiting at the counter (`wg.Wait()`) until both are ready!

**Line-by-Line Syntax Walkthrough:**
1. `var wg sync.WaitGroup` — Creates a counter to track running goroutines.
2. `wg.Add(1)` — Increments the counter *before* launching the goroutine.
3. `go func(val int) { defer wg.Done(); ... }(n)` — Starts a concurrent goroutine that guarantees `wg.Done()` runs when finished.
4. `for _, n := range nums { sum += n * n }` — Iterates through each number `n` in `nums` and adds its square (`n * n`) to `sum`.

[Intermediate Technical]
Never call `wg.Add(1)` *inside* the `go func()` body—if `wg.Wait()` executes before the child goroutine starts, `Wait()` returns prematurely! Always call `wg.Add(1)` in the parent goroutine before `go func()`, and pass loop variables as arguments (or rely on Go 1.22+ per-iteration loop variable semantics).

[Advanced Internals]
Under the hood, `sync.WaitGroup` packs the 32-bit waiter count and 32-bit task counter into a single 64-bit `atomic.Uint64` word, using `runtime_Semacquire` and `runtime_Semrelease` only when the counter transitions to zero with active waiters.

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: Your step-by-step introduction to Go concurrency (`go` keyword, `sync.WaitGroup`, and channels) before tackling the advanced GMP scheduler and bounded worker pools in Lesson 2.1.
2. Internal Mechanics: Prefixing a function call with `go` schedules a lightweight ~2KB goroutine onto the Go runtime. `sync.WaitGroup` maintains an atomic counter (`Add`, `Done`, `Wait`), and a channel (`chan T`) provides a synchronized queue for passing values between goroutines.
3. Why Needed: Sequential backends wait idly during network I/O (fetching user profile + permissions + billing one by one takes 30ms + 30ms + 30ms = 90ms; running them concurrently takes ~30ms).
4. Why Preferred: Learning `sync.WaitGroup` and simple result collection first prevents the classic beginner mistake of spawning fire-and-forget goroutines that silently vanish or race on shared variables.
5. When To Use: Whenever a handler needs to fan out independent I/O calls or batch-process independent items and wait for all results.
6. When To Avoid: Do not use goroutines for tiny CPU loops (like summing 5 integers in production)—the scheduling overhead exceeds a simple `for` loop! Use concurrency when tasks block on I/O or heavy independent work.
7. Advantages: Simple syntax (`go fn()`), built-in race detector (`go test -race`), and deterministic synchronization via `sync.WaitGroup`.
8. Disadvantages: Forgetting `defer wg.Done()` causes a permanent deadlock; reading/writing the same variable from multiple goroutines without synchronization causes a data race.
9. Alternatives: Sequential `for` loops (simpler and faster for small in-memory slices) or `errgroup.Group` (for concurrent tasks that can return errors).
10. Incorrect Consequences: Modifying a shared `total += n * n` variable from multiple goroutines without a mutex or channel corrupts the sum under concurrent execution (`DATA RACE`).
11. Real-World Usage: Parallelizing independent downstream API calls (e.g., fetching product details and inventory counts simultaneously) while waiting via `sync.WaitGroup`.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: Always bound concurrency in production and run `go test -race ./...` in CI to catch unsynchronized shared memory writes.
lesson_sections.diagram_text: [main goroutine] --(wg.Add(1) + go worker())--> [Worker Goroutines] --(ch <- n*n)--> [Buffered Channel] --> [wg.Wait() + Sum]
lesson_sections.reasoning: For pure in-memory integer math, a sequential `for _, n := range nums` loop is 100% race-free and zero-allocation; when goroutines are used for I/O, collect results over a buffered channel or protect shared state.
lesson_sections.title: 2.0 Concurrency 101: Your First Goroutine, Buffered Channels & sync.WaitGroup

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "A router looks at the incoming URL and HTTP method (like `GET /users/42`) and calls the right Go function. Middleware wraps your functions like layers of an onion to handle logging, security headers, and authentication in one place. Since Go 1.22, Go's built-in `http.ServeMux` can handle methods and `{id}` variables without needing any external library!", "intermediate": "Compare routers by `http.Handler` compatibility: `net/http` and `Chi` use standard `func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)`, whereas `Gin` (`func(*gin.Context)`) and `Echo` (`func(echo.Context) error`) introduce custom context types. For pagination on tables >100k rows, replace `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000` (which forces the DB to scan and discard 100,000 rows) with keyset/cursor pagination (`WHERE (created_at, id) < ($1, $2) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20`).", "advanced": "During a Kubernetes rolling update, Kubernetes sends `SIGTERM` to your container while simultaneously removing its IP from `EndpointSlices`. Because kube-proxy/Ingress updates propagate asynchronously across nodes, your pod may still receive new requests for 1\u20133 seconds after `SIGTERM`. A production shutdown handler traps `SIGTERM`, marks `/readyz` as `503 Service Unavailable`, optionally pauses briefly for load-balancer propagation, and then calls `httpServer.Shutdown(ctx)` so in-flight requests finish cleanly before closing the DB pool."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
HTTP Framework & Router Engineering Trade-Off Spectrum:
┌──────────────────────┬────────────────────┬───────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Router / Framework   │ net/http Compatible│ Context Type      │ Primary Trade-Off & Sweet Spot           │
├──────────────────────┼────────────────────┼───────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Go 1.22+ ServeMux    │ 100% Native        │ context.Context   │ Zero deps; method+wildcard routing built │
│ Chi (go-chi/chi/v5)  │ 100% Native        │ context.Context   │ Sub-routers & middleware groups, 0 lockin│
│ Gin                  │ Custom Wrapper     │ *gin.Context      │ Fast radix tree, huge ecosystem, coupled │
│ Echo                 │ Custom Wrapper     │ echo.Context      │ Ergonomic central error handler          │
│ Fiber                │ NO (uses fasthttp) │ *fiber.Ctx        │ Unsafe zero-alloc reuse, breaks stdlib!  │
└──────────────────────┴────────────────────┴───────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘
lesson_sections.reasoning: Keyset pagination uses a B-Tree index seek on `(created_at DESC, id DESC)` to deliver constant sub-millisecond latency at page 1 or page 50,000. `srv.Shutdown(shutdownCtx)` stops accepting new connections and waits for active handlers to finish.
lesson_sections.title: 3.1 Standard net/http (Go 1.22+) vs Chi, Gin, Echo & Fiber + Middleware & Graceful Shutdown

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
An HTTP Handler in Go is a function with two arguments: `r *http.Request` (the incoming envelope from the user) and `w http.ResponseWriter` (the outgoing reply sheet). Always follow the 3-step reply order on `w`: (1) Set headers (`Content-Type: application/json`), (2) Set the status code (`w.WriteHeader(200)`), and (3) Write the JSON body!

[Intermediate Technical]
In Go 1.22+, `mux := http.NewServeMux()` lets you register `"GET /api/v1/lessons/{id}"` and read `id := r.PathValue("id")`. Standardizing a `WriteJSONResponse(w, status, payload)` helper guarantees every endpoint emits UTF-8 JSON with the right status code.

[Advanced Internals]
Under the hood, `http.ResponseWriter` buffers headers until the first `WriteHeader(code)` or `Write(bytes)` call. If `Write(bytes)` is called first, `net/http` implicitly calls `WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)` and sniffs the first 512 bytes for `Content-Type`, locking the header map.

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: The foundational pattern for building a standard-library HTTP server in Go 1.22+ before comparing external routers or middleware chains.
2. Internal Mechanics: `http.ServeMux` matches the HTTP method and URL path pattern (e.g. `"GET /api/v1/tasks/{id}"`), extracts wildcard segments via `r.PathValue("id")`, and invokes your `http.HandlerFunc(w, r)` on the connection goroutine.
3. Why Needed: Every Go web service is built on the `http.Handler` interface (`ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)`). Mastering it first makes every router and middleware library transparent.
4. Why Preferred: Go 1.22+ `http.ServeMux` supports method routing (`GET`, `POST`, `DELETE`) and path wildcards (`{id}`) in the standard library with zero external dependencies.
5. When To Use: For all REST APIs, health checks, and microservice HTTP boundaries.
6. When To Avoid: Never write to `w` before setting response headers and status code.
7. Advantages: Zero external dependencies; 100% stdlib compatibility; simple testing with `net/http/httptest`.
8. Disadvantages: Requires writing a small helper (`WriteJSON`) for consistent headers and status codes.
9. Alternatives: Chi or Echo when specialized sub-router mounting is needed (covered in Lesson 3.1).
10. Incorrect Consequences: Calling `w.Write()` or `json.NewEncoder(w).Encode()` before `w.Header().Set(...)` and `w.WriteHeader(status)` flushes HTTP `200 OK` with `text/plain`, ignoring your intended status code and `Content-Type`.
11. Real-World Usage: `internal/platform/http/response.go` (`WriteJSON` and `WriteProblem`) in this repository implements this exact pattern.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: Concurrency note: Because each HTTP request runs in its own goroutine, any in-memory map or slice shared by handlers must be guarded by a `sync.RWMutex` or stored in SQLite/PostgreSQL.
lesson_sections.diagram_text: Client Request -> http.NewServeMux ("GET /api/v1/tasks/{id}") -> Handler(w, r) -> w.Header().Set -> w.WriteHeader -> json.NewEncoder(w).Encode
lesson_sections.reasoning: Setting `Content-Type` first, then committing `status` via `w.WriteHeader(status)`, and finally streaming JSON into `w` obeys the HTTP wire protocol order.
lesson_sections.title: 3.0 Building Your First Go HTTP Server: Handlers, ServeMux, Status Codes & JSON CRUD

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "Rate Limiting stops a single user or bot from sending 10,000 requests per second and crashing your server. A Token Bucket gives each user a bucket of tokens (say, 20 tokens) that refills at 10 tokens per second\u2014each request costs 1 token, and when the bucket is empty, the server returns `429 Too Many Requests`.", "intermediate": "When configuring CORS in Go, never reflect `w.Header().Set(\"Access-Control-Allow-Origin\", r.Header.Get(\"Origin\"))` unconditionally! Maintain an explicit `map[string]bool` allowlist of trusted origins, and always set `w.Header().Add(\"Vary\", \"Origin\")` so reverse proxies and CDNs do not serve Origin A's cached headers to Origin B.", "advanced": "For an in-memory per-IP Token Bucket map (`map[netip.Addr]*bucket`) in Go, an attacker rotating through IPv6 addresses can create millions of map entries and OOM-kill your process. Always pair in-memory rate limiters with either a bounded LRU/sharded map or a background cleanup ticker that deletes buckets idle for >5 minutes."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
Token Bucket Rate Limiter (Rate R tokens/sec, Burst Capacity B):
  [Bucket Capacity B = 20 tokens]  <── Refills continuously at R = 10 tokens/sec
       │
       ├── Incoming HTTP Request:
       │     ├── If tokens >= 1: decrement token -> 200 OK (X-RateLimit-Remaining: N)
       │     └── If tokens < 1 : reject immediately -> 429 Too Many Requests (Retry-After: 1)
lesson_sections.reasoning: Checking `allowedOrigins[origin]` against a strict configuration map and always emitting `Vary: Origin` enforces least-privilege cross-origin access and safe proxy caching.
lesson_sections.title: 3.2 Request Validation, Token-Bucket Rate Limiting, CORS Allowlists & OpenAPI 3.1 Contracts

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "A database isn't a magic black box\u2014without an Index, asking for `WHERE email = 'alice@example.com'` forces the database to read every single row on disk (a Sequential Scan). An Index is like a sorted book index (a B-Tree) that jumps straight to the matching row in a few steps. And Transactions (ACID) ensure that if money leaves Account A, it is guaranteed to arrive in Account B, even if the server crashes halfway through.", "intermediate": "Composite B-Tree indexes follow the Leftmost Prefix Rule: an index on `(tenant_id, status, created_at)` accelerates queries filtering on `tenant_id`, `(tenant_id, status)`, or `(tenant_id, status, created_at)`, but cannot be used as a primary index seek for a query filtering only on `status`. Furthermore, understand SQL Isolation Levels: PostgreSQL defaults to `READ COMMITTED` (each statement sees a fresh snapshot committed before that statement began), whereas MySQL InnoDB defaults to `REPEATABLE READ` (snapshot fixed at the first read in the transaction).", "advanced": "In PostgreSQL `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`, inspect `Buffers: shared hit=X read=Y` alongside `actual time` and `loops`. A `Nested Loop` with `loops=500` executes the inner node 500 times (multiply inner `actual time` by `loops`!). Also beware MVCC write skew under `REPEATABLE READ`: two doctors on call simultaneously check `SELECT count(*) FROM doctors WHERE on_call = true` (seeing 2), and both update their own row to `false`. Because they update disjoint rows, `REPEATABLE READ` permits both commits unless you use `SERIALIZABLE` (which detects the rw-antidependency cycle via SSI and aborts one with SQLSTATE `40001`)."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
PostgreSQL MVCC vs MySQL InnoDB Clustered Storage:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ PostgreSQL Heap Page (8KB): Stores Tuple Versions (xmin, xmax, ctid) directly in heap. │
│   • Secondary B-Tree Index points to physical Heap Tuple (ctid).                       │
│   • UPDATE writes a NEW tuple version (unless Heap-Only Tuple / HOT applies);          │
│     Autovacuum reclaims dead tuples later. Readers NEVER block writers!                │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ MySQL InnoDB Page (16KB): Table IS a Clustered B+Tree ordered by PRIMARY KEY.          │
│   • Secondary Index leaf stores the PRIMARY KEY value (requires double B+Tree lookup). │
│   • UPDATE modifies row in-place and writes old version to Undo Log for MVCC reads.    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
lesson_sections.reasoning: The `WHERE id = $2 AND balance >= $1` predicate acquires an exclusive row-level lock on the target tuple and re-evaluates the condition after any concurrent transaction commits, guaranteeing that `balance` can never drop below zero.
lesson_sections.title: 4.1 Relational vs NoSQL Internals, MVCC, ACID Isolation Levels, Indexing & EXPLAIN ANALYZE

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "Partitioning splits one giant table (like `logs` with 500 million rows) into monthly sub-tables (`logs_2026_10`, `logs_2026_11`) inside the same database so queries only look at the current month. Replication copies your database to backup read-only servers so if the main server dies, a standby server takes over.", "intermediate": "Beware the **Read-Your-Own-Writes** anomaly with asynchronous Read Replicas: a user updates their profile on the Primary DB and their browser immediately reloads the page, hitting a Read Replica that is 50ms behind. The user sees their old profile and thinks the save failed! Fix this by routing a user's reads to the Primary for a short window (e.g. 3 seconds) after any write, or by comparing the Primary's `pg_current_wal_insert_lsn()` against the Replica's `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()`.", "advanced": "Why is `DROP TABLE logs_2025_01` on a partitioned table 10,000x faster than `DELETE FROM logs WHERE created_at < '2025-02-01'`? Because `DELETE` in PostgreSQL must visit every row, mark its `xmax` transaction ID, write WAL records for all 50M rows, and leave dead tuples behind for `VACUUM` to clean up\u2014whereas `DETACH` + `DROP` simply unlinks the partition's underlying OS file descriptors!"}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
PostgreSQL WAL Streaming Replication & Read-Your-Own-Writes Consistency:
[Go API] ── 1. INSERT order (Primary DB commits & appends LSN 0/16B3748 to WAL) ──► [Primary Postgres]
   │                                                                                        │
   │ 2. Immediate GET /orders (Routed to Read Replica BEFORE LSN 0/16B3748 replays!)        │ Async WAL Stream
   └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────► [Read Replica (LSN 0/16B3600)]
   (Fix: Stick user to Primary for 2s after write, OR wait for pg_last_wal_replay_lsn() >= write_lsn!)
lesson_sections.reasoning: Pinning a user session to the Primary pool for `safeReplicationWindow` (or until replica WAL replay LSN catches up) preserves causal consistency while still offloading 95%+ of general read traffic to replicas.
lesson_sections.title: 4.2 Streaming Replication Lag, Declarative Partitioning, Sharding & Point-in-Time Recovery (PITR)

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
Think of a Relational Database as a set of connected spreadsheets (Tables) with strict guardrails. `customers` holds one row per person with a unique `id` (**Primary Key**). `orders` holds purchases and points back to `customer_id` (**Foreign Key**). `SELECT` picks columns, `WHERE` filters rows, `JOIN` connects `customers` with their `orders`, and `GROUP BY` sums totals per customer.

[Intermediate Technical]
Normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF) eliminates redundant data: instead of repeating `customer_email` on every order row (which goes stale when a customer changes their email), `orders` stores `customer_id REFERENCES customers(id)`. Use `INNER JOIN` when both sides must match, and `LEFT JOIN` with `COALESCE` when you also want customers with zero orders.

[Advanced Internals]
In both PostgreSQL and SQLite, declaring `PRIMARY KEY` or `UNIQUE` automatically creates a B-Tree index, but declaring a `FOREIGN KEY` does NOT automatically index the child column! Always create an explicit index on foreign key columns (like `idx_orders_customer_status_created`) to avoid full-table scans on joins and `ON DELETE CASCADE`.

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: The foundational language (SQL) and relational model used by PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL, and MariaDB to store, constrain, join, and aggregate persistent data.
2. Internal Mechanics: Data is organized into relations (tables) with typed columns. Primary Keys enforce row identity via a unique B-Tree index; Foreign Keys enforce referential integrity across tables; `CHECK` and `NOT NULL` reject invalid data inside the database engine.
3. Why Needed: Before you can understand MVCC tuple visibility or B-Tree page splits (Lesson 4.1), you must know how to model tables and write `SELECT`, `JOIN`, `GROUP BY`, and bounded `LIMIT` queries.
4. Why Preferred: Declarative SQL with schema constraints guarantees data integrity even if multiple services or scripts access the database.
5. When To Use: Whenever domain entities have structured relationships (users, orders, order_items, payments, progress).
6. When To Avoid: Never store comma-separated lists in a single column (violates 1NF) or run unbounded `SELECT *` queries without a `LIMIT`.
7. Advantages: Strict schema enforcement (`PRIMARY KEY`, `FOREIGN KEY`, `UNIQUE`, `CHECK`); expressive joins and aggregations.
8. Disadvantages: Requires upfront schema design and versioned SQL migrations (`migrations/*.sql`).
9. Alternatives: Document or key-value stores when records are self-contained blobs with no cross-entity joins.
10. Incorrect Consequences: Allowing unbounded `LIMIT` or negative `OFFSET` values from query parameters lets a single client request scan millions of rows and crash the database.
11. Real-World Usage: Go Backend Academy uses 20 normalized tables in `migrations/sqlite/001_initial_schema.up.sql` and `migrations/postgres/001_initial_schema.up.sql`.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: Scalability: Always clamp pagination `LIMIT` (e.g. default 20, max 100) and index Foreign Key columns.
lesson_sections.diagram_text: [customers (id PK, email UNIQUE)] 1 <--- * [orders (id PK, customer_id FK, status, total_cents)] ---> SELECT ... LEFT JOIN ... GROUP BY
lesson_sections.reasoning: Enforcing a sensible default (20), hard ceiling (100), and non-negative offset bounds the worst-case memory and I/O cost of any list query.
lesson_sections.title: 4.0 SQL from Scratch: Tables, Primary/Foreign Keys, SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY & Normalization

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "In Go, you have four main ways to talk to a SQL database: 1) Raw SQL (`database/sql` or `pgx`), where you write SQL and scan columns into variables yourself; 2) Code Generation (`sqlc`), where you write SQL and a tool generates type-safe Go functions for you; 3) Query Builders (`Bun`), where you chain helper methods; and 4) ORMs (`GORM`), which map Go structs to tables automatically at runtime.", "intermediate": "Always remember that `*sql.DB` is NOT a single connection\u2014it is a thread-safe pool of connections created once at startup and shared across the application. When iterating over `rows, err := db.QueryContext(ctx, ...)`, you MUST call `defer rows.Close()` immediately after checking `err != nil`, and check `rows.Err()` after the `for rows.Next()` loop finishes.", "advanced": "Compare the same `GetUserOrders` operation across all four approaches: `GORM`'s `db.Preload(\"Orders\").First(&user, id)` executes two queries and uses `reflect.Value` allocation per field; `sqlc` compiles your SQL `JOIN` or `json_agg` query into direct `row.Scan(&item.ID, &item.Total)` calls over `pgx/v5`'s binary protocol, running 3x\u20135x faster with 70% fewer heap allocations per row."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
Go Database Access Layer Trade-Off Matrix:
┌──────────────────┬─────────────────┬─────────────────┬──────────────────┬────────────────────────┐
│ Tool / Library   │ Type Safety     │ Runtime Overhead│ SQL Control      │ Ideal Engineering Fit  │
├──────────────────┼─────────────────┼─────────────────┼──────────────────┼────────────────────────┤
│ database/sql     │ Manual Scan()   │ Low             │ 100% Raw SQL     │ Portable multi-DB code │
│ jackc/pgx/v5     │ Manual / Collect│ Lowest (Binary) │ 100% Postgres SQL│ High-perf Postgres APIs│
│ sqlc             │ Compile-Time Gen│ Lowest (ZeroRef)│ 100% Raw SQL     │ Production Go Standard │
│ Bun              │ Struct Tags     │ Low-Medium      │ High (SQL-first) │ Dynamic filter builders│
│ Ent              │ Codegen Graph   │ Medium          │ Medium (DSL)     │ Deep graph traversals  │
│ GORM             │ Runtime Reflect │ Highest         │ Medium (Hooks)   │ Rapid CRUD prototypes  │
└──────────────────┴─────────────────┴─────────────────┴──────────────────┴────────────────────────┘
lesson_sections.reasoning: `defer rows.Close()` ensures the underlying network socket is returned to `*sql.DB`'s idle pool even if `rows.Scan` fails or the context is canceled mid-iteration. Checking `rows.Err()` catches broken TCP pipes during cursor streaming.
lesson_sections.title: 5.1 database/sql vs pgx/v5 vs sqlc vs GORM vs Ent vs Bun & Pool Internals

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "Never call an outside API (like sending an email or charging a credit card over HTTP) *inside* an open database transaction (`tx`)! While your Go code waits 2 seconds for the outside API to reply, that database connection and its locked rows are frozen, quickly using up all connections in your pool.", "intermediate": "When adding an index to a large production PostgreSQL table, always use `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_name ON table(col);` so writes are not blocked. Note that `CONCURRENTLY` cannot run inside a `BEGIN ... COMMIT` transaction block, so your migration runner must support non-transactional migration steps when needed.", "advanced": "Why does PostgreSQL's lock queue cause sudden 100% outages during seemingly harmless `ALTER TABLE` statements? Because `ALTER TABLE` requests an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock. If a 10-second analytical `SELECT` is currently running on that table, `ALTER TABLE` waits in the lock queue\u2014and PostgreSQL's lock fairness rules block *every new `SELECT`, `INSERT`, and `UPDATE`* behind the waiting `ALTER TABLE`! Always prepend `SET lock_timeout = '2s';` to every DDL migration so it aborts cleanly if it cannot acquire the lock immediately."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
Expand-and-Contract Zero-Downtime Schema Migration (Renaming/Changing a Column):
  Phase 1 (Expand)  : ADD new nullable column + trigger/dual-write in Go v1.1 (Old v1.0 pods still work!)
  Phase 2 (Backfill): Batch-update historical rows in small 5,000-row chunks (avoids long table lock)
  Phase 3 (Switch)  : Deploy Go v1.2 reading from new column + validate constraint NOT VALID -> VALIDATE
  Phase 4 (Contract): DROP legacy column in a subsequent release once zero pods reference it
lesson_sections.reasoning: Splitting the workflow into two 1ms database state transitions around the external HTTP call reduces database connection hold time from ~2,000ms to ~2ms (a 1,000x increase in connection pool capacity).
lesson_sections.title: 5.2 Expand-and-Contract Zero-Downtime SQL Migrations, Prepared Statements & Transaction Scopes

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
To talk to a SQL database from Go, you use `*sql.DB`. There are 3 main methods: (1) `ExecContext` to change data (`INSERT`/`UPDATE`/`DELETE`), (2) `QueryRowContext` to fetch 1 row, and (3) `QueryContext` to fetch many rows. Never glue user strings into SQL—always write `$1` in the SQL and pass the variable as an argument!

[Intermediate Technical]
When fetching a single row with `db.QueryRowContext(ctx, q, arg).Scan(&dest)`, `database/sql` returns `sql.ErrNoRows` if no row matched. Translate `errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows)` into a domain `ErrNotFound` so your HTTP layer can return `404 Not Found` instead of `500`.

[Advanced Internals]
For multi-step writes, call `tx, err := db.BeginTx(ctx, nil)`, immediately schedule `defer func() { _ = tx.Rollback() }()`, run all `tx.ExecContext` statements, and finish with `return tx.Commit()`. Once `Commit()` succeeds, the deferred `Rollback()` is a safe no-op.

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: Practical day-to-day usage of Go standard `database/sql` package for safe CRUD queries and transactions before comparing ORMs or code generators.
2. Internal Mechanics: `sql.Open(driver, dsn)` initializes a lazy, thread-safe connection pool (`*sql.DB`). `db.PingContext(ctx)` verifies connectivity. `QueryRowContext`, `QueryContext`, and `ExecContext` borrow a connection from the pool, bind parameters separately from SQL text, and return the connection when `Scan` or `rows.Close()` finishes.
3. Why Needed: Every persistent Go backend must read and write SQL rows without leaking connections or exposing SQL injection vulnerabilities.
4. Why Preferred: Standard `database/sql` works identically across `modernc.org/sqlite` and `jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib` using `$1` positional placeholders.
5. When To Use: For all SQL queries, repository methods, and multi-statement atomic transactions (`db.BeginTx`).
6. When To Avoid: Never build SQL queries with `fmt.Sprintf` or string concatenation `+` on user input, and never call `db.QueryContext` without `defer rows.Close()`.
7. Advantages: Parameter binding prevents user values from being interpreted as SQL commands. Table/column names and ORDER BY cannot be parameterized (use allowlists); context-aware timeouts; built-in connection pooling.
8. Disadvantages: Manual `rows.Scan(&a, &b)` column order must match the `SELECT` list.
9. Alternatives: `sqlc` (generates type-safe Go from SQL) or `pgx/v5` native interface (compared in Lesson 5.1).
10. Incorrect Consequences: Jika rows tidak ditutup dan iterasi berhenti sebelum Next() mengembalikan false (mis. return lebih awal atau break), koneksi database tetap terpakai sampai rows.Close() dipanggil. Selalu defer rows.Close() dan periksa rows.Err() setelah loop.
11. Real-World Usage: Look at `internal/platform/database/db.go` and `content.go` in this repository—every single query uses `QueryContext`/`QueryRowContext`/`ExecContext` with `$1` parameters and `defer rows.Close()`.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: Security: `$1` parameter placeholders prevent SQL injection. Reliability: `defer tx.Rollback()` before `tx.Commit()` guarantees transactions never stay open on error.
lesson_sections.diagram_text: *sql.DB Pool -> db.QueryRowContext(ctx, "SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = $1", email).Scan(&id) -> errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows)
lesson_sections.reasoning: `QueryRowContext` with `$1` binds `email` safely, releases the pooled connection immediately inside `Scan`, and maps `sql.ErrNoRows` to `ErrUserNotFound`.
lesson_sections.title: 5.0 Connecting Go to SQL: database/sql, QueryContext, Scan, Parameterized Queries & Transactions

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "OAuth 2.0 lets users log in via a trusted provider without giving your app their password, and OpenID Connect (OIDC) gives your Go backend a signed ID card (ID Token). RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) groups permissions into roles like `viewer`, `editor`, and `billing_admin` so you check permissions (`HasPermission(role, \"invoice:delete\")`) instead of scattering `if user.Role == \"admin\"` everywhere.", "intermediate": "When verifying JWTs or webhook HMAC signatures during a secret rotation, your Go server must accept **both** the `current` key and the `previous` key during a transition window (e.g., 24 hours). Sign all new tokens with the `current` key (`kid: \"key-2026-11\"`), while allowing verification to look up `kid` in a map containing both `key-2026-11` and `key-2026-10`.", "advanced": "Critical OIDC Security Check: Signature verification alone is NEVER sufficient! If two microservices or two client apps share an OAuth2/OIDC issuer, an attacker can take a validly signed JWT intended for `aud: \"analytics-viewer\"` and send it to `aud: \"payments-service\"`. Always assert exact `iss` match, `aud` membership, `exp > now - skew`, and `alg` allowlist."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code + PKCE & OIDC JWKS Verification Flow:
[Client] ── 1. code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(code_verifier)) ──► [Identity Provider (IdP)]
[Client] ── 2. Exchanges code + plaintext code_verifier ──────────► [Go Backend / Token Endpoint]
[Go API] ── 3. Fetches & Caches IdP /.well-known/jwks.json (Key ID "kid")
         └──► Verifies RS256/EdDSA Signature, iss, aud, exp & Tenant RBAC Permissions
lesson_sections.reasoning: Validating `Issuer`, `Audience`, `Expires`, and `Subject` deterministically after cryptographic signature verification ensures tokens cannot be replayed across unintended services.
lesson_sections.title: 6.2 OAuth 2.0 with PKCE, OpenID Connect (JWKS), RBAC vs ABAC & Secrets Rotation

lesson_sections.body_text: {"beginner": "Never store plain-text passwords! Hash them with Argon2id or bcrypt so even if your database leaks, attackers only see slow, salted hashes. Never glue user input directly into a SQL string (`\"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '\" + input + \"'\"`)\u2014always use placeholders (`$1`) so the database treats user input strictly as data, never as executable SQL commands.", "intermediate": "Every OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) risk maps to concrete Go defenses: API1 (BOLA) -> scope every query by `WHERE id = $1 AND tenant_id = $2`; API2 (Broken Auth) -> pin JWT signing algorithms and enforce constant-time comparison; API3 (Broken Object Property Level Auth / Mass Assignment) -> use dedicated request DTO structs rather than binding JSON directly into database model structs containing `IsAdmin bool`; API7 (SSRF) -> block loopback, link-local (`169.254.0.0/16`), and private RFC 1918 IPs.", "advanced": "Why does URL-string validation fail against SSRF? Because of DNS Rebinding (TOCTOU): when your validator resolves `evil.example.com`, the attacker's DNS server returns `93.184.216.34` (public IP) with `TTL=0`. Milliseconds later, when `http.Client.Do(req)` dials `evil.example.com`, the DNS server returns `127.0.0.1` or `169.254.169.254`. The only bulletproof defense in Go is attaching a `Control` callback to `net.Dialer` inside `http.Transport.DialContext`, which inspects the actual resolved `syscall.RawConn` address (`netip.Addr`) immediately before `connect()`."}
lesson_sections.diagram_text:
Short-Lived Access JWT + Stateful Refresh Token Rotation Flow:
[Client] ── 1. POST /auth/login (Email + Password verified via Argon2id constant-time) ──► [Go Auth Service]
         ◄─ 2. Returns: Access JWT (5 min TTL, EdDSA/ES256) + HttpOnly Refresh Token (7d) ─┘
[Client] ── 3. API Request with Authorization: Bearer <Access JWT> (Verified statelessly) ─► [Go Resource API]
[Client] ── 4. POST /auth/refresh (Rotates Refresh Token Family in DB; revokes family on reuse!)
lesson_sections.reasoning: `netip.ParseAddr` checks loopback (`127.0.0.1`, `::1`), RFC 1918 private ranges (`10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`), and cloud metadata link-local addresses (`169.254.169.254`). Running this inside `net.Dialer.Control` neutralizes DNS rebinding.
lesson_sections.title: 6.1 Argon2id, JWT vs Sessions, OAuth2/OIDC, RBAC, SQLi/SSRF/XSS/CSRF & OWASP API Top 10

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
When you log into an app, the server gives your browser a digital badge called a **Bearer Token**. Every time your browser asks for private data, it shows that badge in an HTTP header: `Authorization: Bearer abc123xyz`.

**Line-by-Line Syntax Walkthrough:**
1. `const prefix = "Bearer "` — Defines the exact 7-character prefix required by RFC 6750.
2. `if !strings.HasPrefix(authHeader, prefix) { return "", false }` — Safely rejects any header that does not start with `"Bearer "` (no slice index panics!).
3. `tok := strings.TrimSpace(strings.TrimPrefix(authHeader, prefix))` — Removes `"Bearer "` and any extra spaces.
4. `return tok, tok != ""` — Returns the token and `true` only if the remaining token is non-empty.

[Intermediate Technical]
Why does `strings.Split(h, " ")[1]` crash production servers? Because an attacker sending `Authorization: Basic` (no space) causes `strings.Split` to return a 1-element slice, triggering a runtime panic! `strings.HasPrefix` + `strings.TrimPrefix` is 100% panic-proof.

[Advanced Internals]
After extracting the bearer token string without allocations, pass it to your JWT verifier (enforcing `alg`, `iss`, `aud`, `exp`) or hash it with SHA-256 to look up the server-side session row.

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: The foundational gateway to backend security: how passwords are stored safely as salted one-way hashes and how HTTP APIs authenticate requests using `Authorization: Bearer <token>` headers.
2. Internal Mechanics: When a user logs in, the server verifies their password against an Argon2id/bcrypt hash and issues a signed token or session ID. On subsequent API calls, the client sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>`, and middleware extracts the token string after the `"Bearer "` prefix.
3. Why Needed: HTTP is stateless; without a clean, strict token extraction boundary, protected endpoints cannot reliably identify the caller or reject malformed credentials.
4. Why Preferred: Validating the exact `"Bearer "` prefix and rejecting blank or whitespace-only tokens fails closed before any database or cryptographic verification runs.
5. When To Use: On every authenticated REST API middleware chain before parsing JWT claims or looking up session rows.
6. When To Avoid: Do not accept tokens in URL query parameters (`?token=xyz`) for normal API calls because URLs are logged in plaintext by proxies, browsers, and access logs.
7. Advantages: Standard RFC 6750 header format, zero allocation string prefix trimming, and clear `401 Unauthorized` failure semantics.
8. Disadvantages: Bearer tokens grant access to anyone possessing them, so TLS (`HTTPS`) and short expiration times are mandatory.
9. Alternatives: `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` session cookies (often preferred for browser-only web apps).
10. Incorrect Consequences: Using `strings.Split(authHeader, " ")[1]` without checking length panics with `index out of range [1] with length 1` whenever a client sends a malformed `Authorization: Bearer` header!
11. Real-World Usage: Used in the authentication middleware of virtually every production Go REST and gRPC gateway.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: `strings.HasPrefix` + `strings.TrimPrefix` runs in `O(1)` time with zero heap allocations, preventing panic DoS vectors on malformed headers.

lesson_sections.reasoning: `HasPrefix` and `TrimPrefix` never panic on short or malformed inputs and allocate zero intermediate slices.

lesson_sections.body_text:
[Beginner Overview]
How do you make sure a function works on normal inputs, messy inputs, and empty inputs? You write a **Table-Driven Test**—a checklist of `(input -> expected output)` rows!

**Line-by-Line Syntax Walkthrough:**
1. `words := strings.Fields(strings.ToLower(title))` — Converts `title` to lowercase and splits it into clean words, automatically ignoring extra spaces or tabs!
2. `return strings.Join(words, "-")` — Joins the clean words with a single `"-"` hyphen between each word (returning `""` if `words` is empty).

[Intermediate Technical]
Compare `strings.Split(s, " ")` vs `strings.Fields(s)`: `strings.Split("  go  backend ", " ")` produces empty strings `["", "", "go", "", "backend", ""]`, whereas `strings.Fields` returns `["go", "backend"]` cleanly.

[Advanced Internals]
Combine table-driven unit tests (`TestSlugifyTitle`) in Lesson 7.0 with `testing.F` fuzzing in Lesson 7.1 to prove that arbitrary Unicode strings never panic or produce leading/trailing hyphens.

[12 Engineering Decision Pillars]
1. What Is It: The foundational guide to Go unit testing: designing pure functions and testing multiple inputs and edge cases systematically using a table of test cases.
2. Internal Mechanics: Go's `testing` package runs any `func TestXxx(t *testing.T)` in `*_test.go` files. By defining a slice of test cases and iterating with `t.Run(tc.name, ...)`, you test 10 edge cases with a single 5-line assertion loop.
3. Why Needed: Untested backend code breaks silently when edge cases (like extra spaces or mixed case in article titles) hit production.
4. Why Preferred: Adding a new bug regression test to a table-driven test takes 1 line (`{name: "tabs and spaces", in: "  Go   101 ", want: "go-101"}`) instead of copying a 15-line test function.
5. When To Use: For every pure business helper, validator, slug generator, parser, and HTTP handler in your service.
6. When To Avoid: Do not put complex `if/else` branching logic inside the test loop itself—keep test expectations explicit and literal.
7. Advantages: Zero external test framework dependencies (`assert` libraries are optional in Go), fast execution, and isolated subtest filtering.
8. Disadvantages: Requires discipline to keep functions deterministic (passing time or random seeds as arguments).
9. Alternatives: Repetitive copy-pasted `TestCase1`, `TestCase2` functions.
10. Incorrect Consequences: Using `strings.ReplaceAll(strings.ToLower(title), " ", "-")` turns `"  Hello   Go "` into `"--hello---go-"` with ugly leading/consecutive hyphens!
11. Real-World Usage: Used across the Go standard library (`strings_test.go`, `net/http/serve_test.go`) and Go Backend Academy's own `server_integration_test.go`.
12. Perf/Sec/Maint/Scale: `strings.Fields` splits on any run of whitespace characters and trims leading/trailing spaces in a single pass.
